newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian region votes in symbolic election.
newsitem.headline: Russian region votes in symbolic election.

text.p: Russia's dynamic Nizhny Novgorod region voted for a new governor on Sunday in a run-off poll between a Communist and reformist that could have a ripple effect on the course of reforms across the country.

Loudspeaker trucks circled the town from early on Sunday playing rock music and announcing, "People of Nizhny Novgorod! Wake up and go to the polling stations -- don't miss your chance to decide your own future."
On the face of it, the vote is simply to replace Boris Nemtsov, summoned by President Boris Yeltsin in March to join his team as a first deputy prime minister and speed up reforms.

But the election -- a closely fought race between the reformist mayor of Nizhny Novgorod city, Ivan Sklyarov, and Communist Gennady Khodyrev -- is an unofficial referendum on the country's painful transition to a market economy.
The two finished almost neck and neck in the first round two weeks ago. Voting started at 6 a.m. (0200 GMT) on Sunday and ends at 11 p.m. (1900 GMT). Results are expected on Monday.
A casually dressed Sklyarov walked to vote at his polling station with his family and approached a girl to ask her name.
"You may now shake my hand," he told the bemused youngster. "You may be shaking the hand of the future governor."
When asked whether he would continue reforms started by Nemtsov, he said: "Why just Nemtsov's reforms? There were Sklyarov reforms as well and they will certainly continue."
Khodyrev did not show up to vote where he was expected.
Nina Sokolova, secretary of the eletoral commission, said there were 2.8 million eligible voters in the region.
"We want as many people as possible to take part so the future governor, whoever he is, has a solid mandate," she said.
Turnout in the first round was 40 percent. Election analysts have calculated turnout below 46 percent would favour Khodyrev.
Nemtsov, a liberal who pioneered economic change in his region after he became governor in 1991, is now a key member of Yeltsin's reshuffled and revitalised cabinet.

"If people reject reforms in his domain, how can he offer them for the rest of Russia?" the financial newspaper Birzha said. Nemtsov is widely seen as the standard bearer of radical reform and a potential successor to Yeltsin.
Nemtsov transformed Nizhny Novgorod, a city of 1.5 million people on the Volga some 420 km (260 miles) southeast of Moscow.
Clean and businesslike, the city's streets are full of new shops and crowded cafes -- a striking contrast to many other depressed and declining regional centres.
Local Communist leaders noted after the first round that even among regional industrial workers, their traditional electorate, many had supported Nemtsov's reforms.
But the outcome is far from clear. The Communists still have a vast field of disciplined potential voters, many awaiting pay packets due months ago. Support is also strong in rural areas.
The Communists can hope for the votes of many pensioners, who make up a third of the region's population, although Moscow recently fulfilled its promise to pay pension arrears.

Communist officials from Moscow rushed to Nizhny Novgorod to back Khodyrev, 55, who ruled the region as a party chief in the late 1980s and later became a sugar trader. He is also backed, surprisingly, by nationalist maverick Vladimir Zhirinovsky.
Nemtsov visited the region last week to campaign for Sklyarov, who is 49 and less charismatic than his predecessor.
